title: The Cave That Breathes
author: written for Leo
source: Written for this app. The cave is invented; the way it breathes is not.
blurb: A crack in a hillside blows air out on Tuesday and sucks it in on Wednesday. Jem wants to know why.

p: The crack was behind the blackberries, and Jem would never have found it if his hat had not gone in first.

It was that kind of wind — the sort that comes over a hill sideways and takes things off your head for fun. The hat went up, then along, then down into the brambles, and Jem went after it with his sleeves pulled over his hands.
He did not find the hat straight away. What he found was warm air on his face.

That was wrong, and he knew it was wrong before he knew why. It was April, and the hillside was cold, and the wind coming over the top of it was colder still. But here, low down, behind a curtain of thorn, something was blowing out at him. Steadily. Not in gusts. Like a person who has been running and is trying not to show it.
Jem went still and let it push against his cheek.

Behind the blackberries the limestone had split. The crack was as tall as he was and no wider than his arm, and it went back into the hill further than the light went. Around its edges the moss grew thicker and greener than anywhere else on the slope, in a neat band, as though someone had planted it there on purpose.
He put his hand flat against the opening. The air moved over his palm and kept moving.
“Where are you coming from?” he said, which was a ridiculous thing to say to a hole. He said it anyway.

His hat was three metres further in, caught on a spur of rock, quite dry. He fetched it out with a stick and put it back on his head, and then he stood there for eleven more minutes, doing nothing at all, while the hill breathed out on him.
He went home for dinner because he was hungry, which he was always faintly ashamed of afterwards. It seemed to him later that a person who was properly serious would have stayed.
He came back the next afternoon with a plan, three things in a bag, and the beginnings of a theory.

The theory was that the hill was warm inside. He had read that mines are warm at the bottom, and that the deep parts of the earth are hotter than the top, and it seemed to him that a hill with a crack in it might simply be letting out the heat it had. Warm air rises and cold air sinks. That was a thing he was sure of. It explained the moss, too, which would like a warm draught in April very much.
The theory lasted until he was two steps from the blackberries.
There was no air on his face.

He pushed through the thorns and put his hand to the opening, the way he had the day before, and the hill took a slow pull at his fingers and did not give it back. He felt his sleeve lift very slightly towards the dark.
It was breathing in.
Jem sat down on the wet grass with his bag in his lap and said a word he was not allowed to say, quietly, and with real feeling.

Then, because he was the sort of boy he was, he got out the things he had brought. A candle, for seeing. A ball of string, for not getting lost. And a feather, because he had thought — correctly, as it turned out — that a feather would show him which way the air went better than his hand could.
He held the feather at the crack and let go.
It did not fall. It hung for half a second, turned once, and went in, unhurried, like a leaf going down a drain, and the dark took it.
He lit the candle and the flame leaned inwards too, bowing towards the hill, and it stayed bowed.
So: out on Tuesday. In on Wednesday. Same hole, same hill, same boy. Something had changed and it was not the hill.
He wrote that down, because writing a thing down is how you stop yourself pretending you already understand it. Then he underlined the last part twice.

His grandfather's barometer hung in the hall and had hung there for forty years, and in all that time Jem had never once looked at it properly. It was a wooden thing shaped like a shield, with a brass dial and a needle, and beneath the numbers somebody long ago had painted the words RAIN, CHANGE, and FAIR.
“It measures how heavy the air is,” his grandfather said, when Jem finally asked.
Jem thought about that. “Air isn't heavy.”

“There's a column of it on top of your head that goes up for miles. It weighs about as much as a small car.” His grandfather tapped the glass, gently, the way people do. “You don't notice because it's pressing on you from every side at once. But it changes. When a storm is coming the air gets lighter, and this drops. When the weather settles it gets heavier, and this climbs.”
Jem stood very still in the hall with his coat half off.
“Grandad,” he said. “If the air outside gets lighter, what happens to air that's shut in a box?”
“It pushes out a bit. It's heavier than what's outside it now, so it goes where it can.”
“And if the air outside gets heavier?”
“Then it presses in. Same reason, other way round.” His grandfather looked at him properly for the first time. “What have you found?”
“A hole,” said Jem. “A big one, I think. A very big one.”

Because that was the part that had arrived all at once, standing in the hall, like a light coming on in a room he had been feeling his way around for two days. The hill was not warm. The hill was not alive. The hill was a box — an enormous stone box, full of its own air — and the crack behind the blackberries was the only place that air could get in or out.
When the weather went bad and the air outside grew light, the cave pushed. When the weather came good and the air outside grew heavy, the cave pulled.
It was not breathing at all. It was doing arithmetic.
“How big,” said his grandfather slowly, “would a hole have to be, to blow on you for eleven minutes?”
Jem did not know. He very much wanted to.
There were rules, and they were his mother's, and they were not negotiable.

He was not to go alone. He was to take two lights and not one, because a cave with one light is a cave with none the moment it fails. The string was to be tied to something outside that was not going to move. And somebody on the surface was to know the hour he went in and the hour he was expected out, and that somebody was going to be her.
Jem agreed to all of it without arguing, which surprised them both.
His grandfather came, slowly, with a stick, and waited at the entrance where he could see daylight, and that counted as not alone.
The first six metres were a squeeze and Jem did not enjoy them. Then the walls went away.

He knew they had gone away before he could see it. The sound changed. His own breath, which had been coming back at him off the rock, stopped coming back. He raised the lamp and the light went out from him in every direction and did not find anything to land on, and he understood that he was standing at the edge of a room bigger than his school.
The floor was smooth and slightly damp and rolled away downhill like a frozen wave. Where the lamp caught it, it shone.

It was not ice. It was stone, laid down a drop at a time — water coming through the limestone above, carrying a little dissolved rock, leaving it behind when it dried. Drop, and a film thinner than paper. Drop, and another. The wave under his boots had taken longer to form than there had been people in the country, and it had happened in the dark, with nobody watching, and it was not finished.
From the ceiling, in the far edge of the light, the same slow water hung in stone teeth.
Jem stood in the middle of it and did the only thing that made sense, which was to hold up the feather.
It hung. It turned once. And it drifted on, further in, into the part he had not seen yet.
The air was still going somewhere. And somewhere, he thought, is not the same as nowhere.
On the third visit he brought a brush, which his grandfather had suggested and which turned out to be the most useful thing he owned.
The walls of the big room were limestone, and limestone is not really rock in the way granite is rock. Granite was molten once. Limestone was alive.

Jem had read the sentence three times before it went in. Limestone is made of shells. Not shells like the ones on the beach — shells too small to see, millions upon millions of them, animals that lived in a warm shallow sea and died and sank and settled, and were pressed by the weight of everything that settled after them, until they were stone.
The hill was a graveyard so old and so full that it had turned into a hill.

He found the first one by accident, with his shoulder. A ridge in the wall where the wall should have been flat. He brushed it, and brushed it again, and out of the grey came a spiral the size of his thumbnail, wound perfectly, chamber inside chamber, exactly the way a shell winds today.
He put his finger on it and then took his finger off, because it felt rude.
“Something was here,” he said out loud, in the enormous dark, and his voice did not carry the way it would have outside.

Not on this hill. There had been no hill. There had been water over all of it, warm as a bath and lit right down to the floor, and this small ribbed thing had gone about its business in it, and had not been thinking about Jem, who would not exist for a length of time that the word *long* does not begin to cover.
He found eleven more before his grandfather called down the passage that it had been an hour.
On the way out he stopped where the squeeze began and held up the feather one last time, for the pleasure of it, and this time it did something new.
It went sideways.
Not in. Not out. Across the passage and into a black seam in the wall that Jem had walked past three times without once looking at.

The seam was narrow and it was the wrong shape and Jem was not going into it, and he knew that within four seconds of putting the lamp to it. It shrank. You could get your shoulders in and then you would find out that you could not get them out, and there is a particular sort of person who finds that out, and Jem intended not to be one.
But the air went in. That was the thing.

He spent a week on it. He wrote in his book every day, the date and the barometer reading from the hall and which way the hole was blowing, and by the end of the week he had a column of numbers and a column of arrows and they agreed with each other every single time. Needle falling: hole blows out. Needle rising: hole sucks in. Nine days, nine matches, no exceptions.
He was extremely pleased with himself for about a day and a half.
Then he noticed the problem, and the problem was the size of it.

The crack behind the blackberries was the width of his arm. The cave was bigger than his school. And when the weather turned, the whole of that enormous room had to empty or fill through one gap you could not fit a bicycle down — which meant the air should have come screaming out of it. A gale. Something you could hear from the path.
It did not scream. It pushed, steadily, politely, for hours.
Jem sat on the wet grass with his book on his knees and worked at it with a pencil, and did not get it, and did not get it, and then got it so suddenly that he said “oh” out loud to nobody.
The air was not being forced through one small gap.
It was going in one and out of another.

Somewhere else on this hill — round the shoulder of it, under the bracken, behind another curtain of thorn nobody had pushed through — there was a second mouth. And the cave was not a box at all. It was a pipe. And a pipe does not have to shout, because a pipe has somewhere to send things.
He stood up so fast his book fell in the grass.
It took him eleven days to find it, and he found it with smoke.

Fire was not allowed, so what he had instead was a tin, and in the tin a smouldering knot of damp grass that his grandfather lit for him at the blackberry crack while Jem walked the hill with a whistle in his pocket. The smoke went into the hill white and thick and unhurried, and Jem went round the shoulder of the slope with his eyes on the ground and his heart going like a bird.
Nothing. Nothing. Bracken, rabbit holes, a fence post, nothing.
He was almost at the far side, in the part where the hill goes down to the road and nobody bothers to walk, when he saw it come out of the ground.

A thread of white, rising out of a fold in the turf as though the hill were smoking a pipe, in a place with no crack, no cave, no hole that anybody would ever have looked twice at. Just grass, and a dip, and a slow ribbon of his grandfather's smoke coming up out of the earth four hundred metres from where it went in.
Jem blew the whistle so hard it hurt his ears.

Later — much later, after the caving club had come with proper lights and proper ropes, after the survey and the argument about the name, after his grandfather had been brought to the entrance in a chair he complained about the whole way and had sat there with his hand flat against the rock and said nothing for a long time — Jem thought about what he had actually found.
Not a cave. Anybody could find a cave; he had found that in the first four minutes, looking for a hat.

What he had found was that the hill was a single thing. The crack and the fold in the turf and the room like a frozen wave and the small ribbed animal in the wall and the needle in his grandfather's hall — all of it one arrangement, working, whether or not there was anybody in it. The hill had been doing this every time the weather turned for longer than there had been anyone to notice. It had breathed through the war. It had breathed through every dull Tuesday of Jem's life.
It was breathing now, while he stood outside in the rain with a whistle in his hand, and it would go on after.
That was the part he could not get to the bottom of, and he did not want to. Some things are better kept as a door you can open again.
He still has the feather. It is in the back of the book, with the nine days of arrows, and it is a little bent.
